title: Priests' Rooms and the Holy Boundary
overview: Ezekiel's guide shows him the rooms where priests eat their share of the offerings and change their clothes, then measures a large square wall that marks off the temple's holy ground from everything else.

parts.label: Rooms on the north side (vv. 1-9)
parts.note: Beside the temple courtyard stood a long block of rooms three floors high, with the upper floors narrower than the lower ones. The Hebrew here is very hard to follow, so exactly how the building looked is unclear even to experts.

parts.label: Matching rooms on the south (vv. 10-12)
parts.note: A second block of rooms on the south side mirrored the northern one in size, doors and passageways. This balance fits the careful symmetry found throughout the temple vision.

parts.label: Where priests eat and change (vv. 13-14)
parts.note: Some offerings counted as most holy: grain offerings, offerings for wrongdoing and offerings to make amends, and priests could eat their share of these only in these rooms. Priests also had to leave their special work clothes here before going out among the people, so what belonged to the sacred space stayed there.

parts.label: The whole area measured (vv. 15-20)
parts.note: The guide measures a perfect square, 500 units on each side, with a wall marking where holy ground ends and ordinary ground begins. The Hebrew says 500 reeds, an area bigger than ancient Jerusalem, while an early Greek translation says 500 cubits (about 250 meters), which many modern scholars think fits the rest of the vision better.

disagreement: Christians differ over what this whole temple vision points to: a literal temple still to be built in the future, a symbolic picture of God's people (which many Christians read in light of Jesus and the church), or an ideal plan meant to shape worship for Jews returning from exile.
think: Is there anything in your own life you deliberately keep separate from the ordinary, and what would change if that boundary disappeared?
